en: The Sutra on the King of Gandhāra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Parthian Kingdom during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with...
He was accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a king named Gandha who served a brāhmaṇa.
This brāhmaṇa lived in the mountains and had planted many fruit trees.
At that time, there was a woodcutter who damaged and destroyed his fruit trees. When the Brahmin saw this, he took him to the king's presence and said, "This man has acted without propriety;
he has ravaged my fruit trees. Your Majesty should punish him by execution."
The king, out of respect for the brahmin, did not dare disobey him and immediately had the tree-feller executed.
Not long thereafter, a cow ate someone’s rice; its owner pursued it and beat it until one horn was broken, and blood flowed down its face so that its pain became unbearable.
The ox went to the king's presence and said, "I was truly without cause for offense when I ate a small amount of this man's rice; now, because of it, I have been beaten and my horns broken."
The owner of the rice also pursued them to where the king was.
Since the king understood the languages of birds and beasts, he said to the ox,
"I shall punish you for killing him."
The ox replied, "Even though you kill this man now, you cannot make me not feel pain; however, you should simply issue a strict command that in the future you do not take another person like me."
The king was moved by these words and said:
"I serve the brahmins, yet it is they who, sitting beneath fruit trees, cause me to kill men; they are not like this ox."
He then called out to the brahmin and asked,
"What merit is there in practicing this path now?
The brahmin replied:
"One may avert calamities and bring about blessings, achieving wealth, honor, and long life.
The King asked again:
"Can one escape from birth and death?"
He replied,
"One cannot escape from birth and death.
The king thought to himself alone:
“What should be done with this path?
He then commanded his ministers to prepare the carriage.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself on the ground before the Buddha and paid him homage, saying:
"I have heard that the Buddha-way is most supreme, its sublime teaching delivering countless beings throughout the world.
I pray that you will accept me as a recipient of the Dharma words, so that I may reform my conduct."

The Buddha immediately conferred upon the king the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, and explained that throughout all heaven, earth, and among humans and things, there is none who does not die.
The king prostrated himself with his head to the ground in salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that I have received the Honored One’s Dharma-precepts, what merit shall I obtain?"
The Buddha said:
"Through giving and observing the precepts, one obtains blessings in the present life;

as for those who practice patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, their merit is immeasurable. After death, they shall ascend to the heavens above, may become a Cakravartin King, and may also attain the unconditioned Way that transcends the world."
The Buddha immediately manifested his physical marks, majestic power, and radiant glory for the king. The king was filled with joy and his mind was liberated; he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, paid homage to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"What was the original cause and condition between this king and the ox?"
When the ox spoke, his mind was immediately enlightened; he abandoned the Brahmin life to follow the Buddha-way, and upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he attained the fruit of the Path.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the king and the ox were brothers. They both became lay disciples (upāsakas) and together observed the fast for one day and one night."
The King upheld the Dharma with diligent and tireless effort; at the end of his life, he ascended to the heavens, and when his merit was exhausted, he returned as a king.

As a cow, he violated the precepts by eating at night and subsequently suffered the retribution thereof; once his punishment ended, he became a cow again. For a hundred lifetimes he still possessed the memory of his past lives, and thus he came now to awaken the King’s mind.
"Seven days after the ox's death, its life will end and it will be reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha said,
"Disciples of the fourfold assembly!
"One who upholds the fast and precepts must not transgress them.
Upon hearing this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, and spirits were filled with joy; they came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Sutra of the King of Gandhāra.
